chunks: Everything in this book that is narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr has been transmitted by me from my father, and from Muhammad ibn Al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with them both), from Sa'd ibn Abdullah, and Al-Himyari together, from Ayyub ibn Nuh, Ibrahim ibn Hashim, Ya'qub ibn Yazid, and Muhammad ibn Abdul Jabbar, all from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr.

key_terms.أَيُّوبُ بْنُ نُوحٍ: Ayyub ibn Nuh, a narrator in the chain
key_terms.إِبْرَاهِيمُ هَاشِمٌ: Ibrahim ibn Hashim, a narrator in the chain
key_terms.الْحُمَيْرِيُّ: Al-Himyari, a specific narrator identified by his nisba
key_terms.رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا: May Allah be pleased with them two, a honorific used for the two Imams
key_terms.رَوَيْتُهُ: I have narrated it, indicating direct transmission from the author
key_terms.سَعْدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Sa'd ibn Abdullah al-Qummi, a key narrator of hadith
key_terms.مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ أَبِي عُمَيْرٍ: Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, a prominent early Shia scholar and narrator
key_terms.مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْجَبَّارِ: Muhammad ibn Abdul Jabbar, a narrator in the chain
key_terms.يَعْقُوبُ بْنُ يَزِيدَ: Ya'qub ibn Yazid, a narrator in the chain

ai.seo_question: Who are the narrators in the chain for Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr's hadiths in Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih?
ai.summary: This passage exemplifies the rigorous 'tawatur' (concurrency) methodology employed by Shaykh al-Saduq, where multiple independent chains converge on Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, a pivotal figure in the Kufan scholarly tradition. By listing diverse narrators such as al-Humayri and al-Sadl ibn Abd Allah, the text underscores the robustness and widespread acceptance of these reports within the early Shia hadith corpus, reinforcing their authority in legal and theological matters.
